# CHARACTERS — *The Long Book*

Nine registered. Two leads at equal depth, a world-plot antagonist, a
barrier enforcer who is not the same person, a confidant apiece, an outsider
on the Draw, and two dependents whose lives both plots materially change.

---

## LEAD A — Sahra Ottun

**27. Drawer. Composed to House Nesuir since 1211. Assessed capacity:
fourteen carries — one short of the record in the Long Book.**

### Position in the Draw

She can take anything: salt, rot, fever, blight, souring. Fourteen carries
is freakish; most of the Shelf works at three or four. It is also the reason
her life is not her own, because a capacity that large is an asset large
enough to be pledged. What it costs her, specifically: she lives permanently
at eight or nine of fourteen, which means she is permanently thirsty,
permanently sweet at the wrists, and has a give in both knees at
twenty-seven. What she cannot do: set. Not one span of it. She has spent
eleven years dependent on other people's hands and hating the dependency, and
this is why she asks a setter what a set will cost him before she asks
whether he will do it — a courtesy so unusual that Yannu stops walking the
first time she does it.

### Wound / Want / Need / Lie

- **Ghost.** 1201, the Hungry Year. She was nine. Her grandmother had
  foundered at the eleventh carry in the Nesuir granaries and the seed rotted
  and the middle Nissa did not plant, and the Sarrow — which had nothing —
  fed the Ottun child anyway, out of stock, all winter, and told her, kindly,
  every day, that she would be worth it. She then watched Ines Ottun die
  slowly of blight over three years, ridged nails lifting off the bed,
  hair gone at the temple, saying she was sorry to a room.
- **Wound.** She has been an investment since she was nine and has never once
  been anything else to anyone, including herself.
- **Lie.** *I am the payment. What I owe is what I am, and a person who
  stops paying is a person who was never worth feeding.*
- **Want (external, Lie-driven).** To see the Ottun entry struck out of the
  Long Book in her lifetime — by carries if she can, by the witnessing if she
  cannot. She has a copy of the balance in her own hand and updates it
  quarterly.
- **Need (internal, opposes the Lie).** To find out whether a person can be
  wanted by someone who is not owed anything by her — and to survive
  finding out.
- **Arc: positive.** She begins as a quantity and ends as a person, and the
  price of the transition is that she permanently destroys the quantity.

**The belief she holds in ch 1 that she cannot hold at the end:** *the debt
is mine, and paying it is the only honest thing about me.*

**The scene where Yannu makes it untenable:** ch 23. He tells her what grey
actually is — that he has kept a fraction of every load he has ever passed,
eleven hundred loads over fourteen years, permanently, in his hands, and no
book anywhere records a span of it, and he does not think that makes him
nothing. It is the first time anyone has described a life of unpaid,
unrecorded, uncredited giving as a life. She has no answer. The finishing
blow lands in ch 35, watching Sefa Quenn — a woman with no capacity, no
entry, and no credit — wash the dead of Sarrow-under-Wall by hand, and being
unable to argue that eleven years of Sahra's carries have been worth more to
that village than that bucket.

### Sliders

- **Proactivity 8.** She petitions, calculates, volunteers, extends the
  survey, and at the end proposes the working herself. What looks like
  passivity in Act I is a woman actively choosing the least-bad option every
  single time.
- **Likability 6, rising.** She is blunt to the point of rudeness, refuses
  comfort, and is visibly using people's affection as an accounting entry.
  She is likeable because she is honest about it.
- **Competence 9.** The best drawer on the Shelf and the second-best clerk;
  she can read a ledger faster than the under-reckoners and does.

### Speech pattern

1. **Vocabulary:** plain, trade-specific, numerate. She uses ledger words
   for emotional facts without noticing.
2. **Sentences:** short. Stacked declaratives. Fragments as list items.
3. **Contractions:** yes, always. She is not formal; she is terse.
4. **Tic:** she repeats a number back before agreeing to anything. *"Four
   carries. Say it again."* And she names loads aloud before taking them,
   even alone.
5. **Questions vs statements:** almost all statements. Her questions are
   procedural: *what does it cost you, how long, whose ground.*
6. **Interruption:** she interrupts to correct arithmetic and for no other
   reason.
7. **Metaphor domain:** ledgers, rates, tides, and bodily inventory. She
   describes grief as a rate.
8. **Directness:** total, to a fault. *"Release me."* Not *I wondered
   whether.*

**Example lines.**
- (ch 5, to Yannu, meeting him) "One third. You understand what that is. It's
  eleven more years. Say something."
- (ch 10, to Dovra) "Release me."
- (ch 17, to Halim) "That's the kindest anybody's ever been to me and I'd
  rather you'd shouted."
- (ch 23) "I don't want it struck. I want you. Those are different words and
  I've never used the second one."
- (ch 41) "About two thousand. I hold fourteen. I'm going to do it anyway
  and I want you to be the one, and I need you to say no if you're going to
  say it now."

### Physical habits and tells

- A chipped clay cup she keeps filled and never empties — she drinks
  constantly and it does nothing, and she will not say she is thirsty.
- She does not touch anyone. Not a hand on a sleeve. Eleven years.
- She counts on her fingers under the table, always in fours.
- Whitened cuticles and a permanent pale line at the hairline. Sleeves down
  in company, because of the sweetness at the wrists.
- The Nesuir tally-ring on her left thumb, turned inward so the mark doesn't
  show. She turns it when she is doing arithmetic she does not want to be
  doing.

### Secrets

1. **She has already foundered once.** At twenty-two, working a fever ward
   alone, she went to fifteen and the thirst stopped for four hours before a
   stranger's setter came through and took it off her. Nobody knows. If an
   assessor knew, her rating would be struck, her instalment reduced, and her
   sentence lengthened by a decade — and, worse, the House would never again
   compel her, which means she would lose the only work that pays. Out to
   Yannu in ch 18.
2. **She has been drawing off the books for three years** — free work for fen
   families who cannot pay a rate, unrecorded, in direct breach of the
   composition, which pledges every carry she takes. If Nesuir found out, the
   composition voids for cause and the Sarrow is distrained the same week.
   Nearly found in ch 20.
3. **The one she does not tell anyone until ch 23: she was relieved when she
   signed.** At nineteen the composition looked like a place to put herself —
   a life arranged in advance, with no requirement that anybody choose her.
   She has used the worst thing that ever happened to her family as a hiding
   place, and she has known it for years.

### Independent goal

Not the world plot, and not Yannu: **she wants Yeshin assessed against a
clean line.** She has wanted this since the child's hand cleaned a spoiled
apple at eleven years old, and it is what she is working toward in ch 1,
before the Wallow weeps and before she has met him. It survives the crisis
and it survives the romance, and in ch 45 it is the thing she gets.

---

## LEAD B — Yannu Dral

**33. Setter and warranted wrack-walker of the eastern lobes. Kethren-born.
Grey to the wrist, right hand; to the second knuckle, left. He has passed
about eleven hundred carries in fourteen years and lies about the last two
hundred on his annual assessment.**

### Position in the Draw

He can set anything a drawer can hand him, and he is one of perhaps four
hundred people alive who can. What it costs him, specifically: a
fingerbreadth of feeling per two hundred carries, permanently, and a jump if
he takes it fast. He has lost the smell of smoke (ch 8, four carries in one
pass for a fen family who could not pay). He will lose taste in ch 30. What
he cannot do: hold. He cannot take a load off a drawer and carry it away for
her, cannot store one against a bad day, cannot give any of it back. He can
only pass, and keep what passing keeps.

He is also the only man on the Shelf who has walked the Whiting's eastern
lobes every season for six years, which means he is the only person alive
who knows, in his body rather than from a book, that the ground has been
moving inward.

### Wound / Want / Need / Lie

- **Ghost.** His brother Veth, four years older, sold a twenty-year
  bond-setter's indenture at nineteen to keep the family's terrace in
  Kethren — the family Yannu was in. Veth was worked at factor speed and hit
  full grey at twenty-eight: no touch, no taste, no smell, a man who could
  not feel a wound. In 1210 he asked Yannu to walk him out onto the Whiting.
  Yannu walked him out. Yannu walked back alone.
- **Wound.** He was bought with someone else's hands, and then he was the
  instrument of that person's end, and he has organised his entire life so
  that no one will ever be diminished on his account again.
- **Lie.** *Feeling is a fund you spend. Spend it on nothing that will miss
  it.* In practice: he takes only the sets he judges necessary, refuses the
  lucrative ones rudely so they do not come back, lives alone on a shell
  bank, and forms no attachment that would have anything to lose when he goes
  grey.
- **Want (external, Lie-driven).** An honest map of the Whiting, walked and
  filed, good enough that the House can never again put a setter on ground
  that will take four carries out of him in one pass. He has been at this
  for six years. It is a monument to Veth and it is also a way of being owed
  nothing by anyone.
- **Need (internal).** To learn that being spent *for* someone is not the
  same as being used up *by* someone — that a hoarded life is a ledger too,
  and a meaner one.
- **Arc: positive.** He begins refusing to spend and ends having spent
  everything, on purpose, for a named person and a named reason.

**The belief he holds in ch 2 that he cannot hold at the end:** *grey is
loss, and the decent thing to do with a life like mine is spend as little of
it as possible.*

**The scene where Sahra makes it untenable:** ch 30. A bank gives at the
Wallow and four of the fen crew go under salt-slurry, and Sahra takes
sixteen — two past everything she has — to hold it off them, and Yannu has
to choose between the rule he has kept for nine years and the woman standing
in front of him with the thirst going thin. He takes four carries in one
pass and it jumps and he loses taste for the rest of his life, and he does
not regret it, and that is the crack. Turi finishes the job in ch 34: *"You
didn't keep your hands, boy. You kept your excuse."*

### Sliders

- **Proactivity 7.** Quiet but relentless: he has been falsifying warrants
  for two years to steer the House off dying ground, which is proactivity
  taken to the edge of a crime.
- **Likability 7.** Rude to the rich, unpaid for the poor, funny in about one
  line per chapter, and entirely without self-pity about the thing he is
  losing.
- **Competence 9.** The best walker on the Shelf. He does not round.

### Speech pattern

1. **Vocabulary:** plain and upland-inflected; a handful of Kethren words for
   ground he has no Shelf word for.
2. **Sentences:** subject, verb, object. Longer than Sahra's but never
   subordinate; he does not hedge.
3. **Contractions:** fewer than hers. Formality is a Kethren habit he has
   never lost and it reads as coldness to Amrith people.
4. **Tic:** he refuses to round, including against himself. *"Two hundred and
   eleven paces."* — *"Call it two hundred."* — *"It is two hundred and
   eleven."* He also never uses an intensifier: no *very*, no *really*.
5. **Questions vs statements:** he answers what was asked and stops. His
   questions are almost all about cost.
6. **Interruption:** never. He waits, which people find unnerving.
7. **Metaphor domain:** ground, footing, distance, and absence — how far a
   thing is, whether it will hold, what he can and cannot feel.
8. **Directness:** blunt about facts, silent about wants. He will tell you
   his grey has reached his wrist and will not tell you he wants anything.

**Example lines.**
- (ch 4, to a factor) "You can afford three setters. Hire one who needs it.
  I am not going to be polite about this a second time."
- (ch 7) "Six spans this year. To the wrist on the right. You asked, so
  that's the answer."
- (ch 15) "Past the second knuckle I get nothing. If you need me to know
  you've moved, say so."
- (ch 33) "Twenty years and it raises two hundred and eighty. I am telling
  you the number because you will find it out and I would rather you had it
  from me."
- (ch 45) "I cannot feel your hand. Tell me it is there and I will believe
  you. That is going to be the arrangement now."

### Physical habits and tells

- Gloves off to greet people who cannot price a setter; gloves on for people
  who can. Sahra works this out in ch 13 and it is the first time she likes
  him.
- Salt on everything, heavily, ridiculously, because it is the last taste he
  can find — and never a word of comment about why.
- He paces distances with his eyes, lips moving.
- He tests surfaces with the back of the hand above the second knuckle,
  never the palm.
- Veth's boots on a nail in the hut, in reach of the door.

### Secrets

1. **He has been falsifying warrants for two years** — marking live ground
   dead where he thinks it is finishing, and quietly closing lobes as
   *silting*. He has been managing the Whiting's decline privately because he
   did not believe the House would do it, and people have been hurt by sets
   he refused to warrant. Found by the audit in ch 26 and used against him.
2. **He did not find Veth's boots.** He walked Veth out. Out in ch 34, to
   Turi, and never to anyone else in the book until ch 45.
3. **He is grey past the wrist and has lied about it on his last two
   assessments,** because a walker assessed past the wrist is retired, and
   retirement means the map stops.

### Independent goal

The honest map — walked, filed, and enforced, so that no setter is ever again
worked to full grey for a rich man's cistern. It predates Sahra by six years
and the Wallow crisis by five. In ch 45 he gets a version of it he did not
want: the House adopts the setter-sink and starts drafting *compulsory*
service, which is his map turned into a levy, and he says so out loud on the
last page.

---

## WHY THESE TWO

Not a bond. There are no bonds in this world.

**What Sahra notices about Yannu.**
1. He paces distances with his lips moving and his numbers are always odd,
   because he never rounds in his own favour, and she has spent her life
   among people who round.
2. He takes his gloves off to greet people who could not possibly price a
   setter's grey, and puts them on for people who could. She works out in
   ch 13 that he is hiding how far gone he is from anyone who might use it,
   and showing his bare hands to everyone who cannot.
3. He salts everything past edibility and never once mentions why, and does
   not want to be asked, and is not being brave about it — it is simply the
   last taste there is and he has arranged his plate around it.
4. He turned down the Ammar cistern contract in front of her — four hundred
   carries, a fortune — by being deliberately rude enough that they would not
   come back, and then walked three hours to set for a Kethren family in the
   Undercity for nothing.

**What Yannu notices about Sahra.**
1. She names her loads aloud before she takes them, in the clerk's cadence,
   *two bays of rot, Ferrey granary, third and fourth* — and she does it when
   there is nobody on the floor to hear it. He works out that she has been
   reading herself into a book since she was a child.
2. She keeps a chipped cup filled and never finishes it, and drinks from it
   the way other people touch a scar, and will not say she is thirsty.
3. She is the only drawer in fourteen years who has asked what a set will
   cost *him* before asking whether he will do it. He stops walking.
4. She does not touch anyone. Not once, not a hand on an arm, not in a crowd.
   He notices because he cannot feel most touch anyway, and she is the only
   person he has met who behaves as if she cannot either.

**The shape of it.** She overspends and calls it honesty; he underspends and
calls it decency. Each is the other's correction, and each is drawn first to
the thing that is wrong with the other, because it is the argument they have
been having with themselves for a decade and this is the first time it has
been on the other side of a conversation.

---

## THE WORLD-PLOT ANTAGONIST — Bel Osse

**54. Chief Reckoner of the Reckoning House since 1214.** Would be a problem
if these two had never met, and is still a problem on the last page.

**What she wants and why it conflicts.** She knows by ch 24 that the Whiting
is finished, and she suppresses the finding — seals the survey, keeps the
pair working under warrant, and accelerates collection across the Book. Her
reasoning is not villainy and the book never lets the reader pretend it is:
every obligation on the Shelf is denominated in carries, every carry is
ultimately secured against the Whiting's capacity, and the moment the Shelf
believes the sink has failed, the currency goes, and with it the water
contracts, the granary financing, and the fever wards, inside one season. She
has watched a credit panic. She was twenty-six in the Hungry Year and she
counted the bodies for the House and the number is in her handwriting.

- **Ghost.** 1201. She wrote the Hungry Year's mortality return herself: 4,100
  names, in her own hand, at twenty-six, over eleven weeks.
- **Wound.** She believes she is the only person in the building who
  understands that the arithmetic is what everything else is standing on.
- **Lie.** *A panic kills more people than a truth prevents, so the truth is
  mine to time.*
- **Want.** To hold the currency together long enough to find a second sink
  quietly. (She reopens the Sur Ellun file in ch 24. It is still closed.)
- **Need.** To learn that a truth she is holding is not a truth she is
  managing; it is one she is spending, at interest, out of other people's
  bodies.
- **Arc: negative, and unrepentant.** She loses the argument in ch 44 because
  the rule compels her to credit a witnessed working, and she is already
  drafting compulsory setter-service before the tide is in. She ends the book
  more powerful, with a better instrument, and says the last threatening
  thing in it.
- **Relation to Turi Osse:** her father's younger brother, estranged since
  she certified the ordinance that pensions full-grey setters at a third
  rate. She witnesses his demonstration in ch 39 and his death in ch 40 and
  does not stop being who she is.

**Why she is not the barrier's enforcer.** She has no interest in Sahra's
marriage and would not cross a room to prevent or promote it. Her pressure
on Sahra is impressment and secrecy; Dovra's is the instrument. They
occasionally act in the same direction and never for the same reason, and in
ch 38 they want opposite things on the same day.

---

## THE BARRIER'S ENFORCER — Dovra Nesuir

**62. Matriarch of House Nesuir, the smallest of the three great houses and
the only one carrying an assessment on its own books.** Legitimate interest,
real standing, and no malice available anywhere in her.

- **Ghost.** 1200–1201. Her husband contracted the blight working with Ines
  Ottun on credit against a bad harvest, watched four thousand quarters of
  seed rot, and hanged himself in Ferrey in the spring of the Hungry Year.
  Dovra took the house at forty-three with an unpayable claim and four
  hundred tenants.
- **Wound.** She has spent eighteen years being the person who does the
  arithmetic that other people find distasteful, and she has never once been
  thanked for the fact that Nesuir's tenants have eaten every winter since.
- **Lie.** *Mercy is something you can only afford after the books balance,
  and the books have never balanced.*
- **Want.** Nesuir solvent and the composition executed. She has pledged it
  forward against Nesuir's own obligations to the House; if it voids she must
  call in the fen tenancies to cover, which destroys the same 1,900 people
  the composition protects. She cannot release Sahra even if she wished to,
  and in ch 10 she opens the book and shows her exactly why.
- **Need.** To admit that she has made a person into an instrument because it
  was the only instrument available, and that this is a thing she did, not a
  thing that happened.
- **Arc: flat, hard, and unbroken.** She does not soften, does not die, is
  not exposed. In ch 32 she invokes the acceleration clause the day after
  Sarrow-under-Wall dies, because that is what the clause is for and because
  her exposure has just become lethal. In ch 45 she reads the discharge,
  checks the arithmetic, says "then it is discharged," and goes. She is
  right about the numbers all the way through.
- **Speech:** balanced complete sentences, never raised, always citing the
  instrument by clause. *"Third Order, the second schedule. You may read it
  yourself; I have marked it."*

---

## CONFIDANT (Sahra) — Ansa Rask

**40. Fen-reeve of the Sarrow, elected three times.** The person Sahra talks
to, and the one whose interest in the answer is disqualifying, which is the
point.

- **Ghost.** She held the Sarrow's stock-book through the Hungry Year at
  twenty-two and decided who ate.
- **Wound.** She has never stopped being a person who divides a finite
  quantity among named children.
- **Lie.** *If I can keep the number of dead low enough, the arithmetic is
  moral.*
- **Want.** The Sarrow's tenure secure and Sahra safe, in that order, and she
  is honest that it is in that order.
- **Need.** To stop mistaking triage for a philosophy.
- **What she wants for Sahra that Turi does not want for Yannu:** she wants
  Sahra married. She says so. *"If you break it, they lose the fen and the
  fen loses you. I love you and I need you married. Both are true and I'm not
  going to pretend the second one away."* (ch 29)
- **Speech:** everything is a headcount. Every position she takes arrives as
  a number of people.

---

## CONFIDANT (Yannu) — Turi Osse

**66. Full-grey setter, pensioned at a third rate since 1216. Lives at the
Kell Ammar salt-house and mends nets by sight.** Bel Osse's uncle.

- **Ghost.** Forty-one years of sets, the last eleven of them for factors,
  and a wife who left in 1198 because he could no longer feel her and would
  not talk about it.
- **Wound.** He is the evidence for the book's central fact — that a setter
  keeps what he passes — and he has said so out loud for thirty years in
  language everyone hears as sentiment.
- **Lie.** *I was used up, so what is left of me is not worth a decision.*
- **Want.** To be believed about one thing before he dies.
- **Need.** Nothing, in the end. He gets the want. It kills him.
- **Arc:** he speaks the theme in ch 2 (*"Nothing's been paid, boy. It's only
  been put somewhere."*), volunteers for the demonstration in ch 37, takes
  four carries out of the Whiting's crust in ch 39 at the cost of sensation
  from the chest inward, and dies on the second tide in ch 40 of cold he
  could not feel. He is not saved and he is not resurrected.
- **What he wants for Yannu that Ansa does not want for Sahra:** he wants him
  to spend it. All of it, on something, before he is too grey to choose.
  *"You didn't keep your hands, boy. You kept your excuse."* (ch 34)
- **Speech:** obscene, funny, exact. Uses the second person for general
  truths.

---

## THE OUTSIDER ON THE SYSTEM — Sefa Quenn

**58. Washer, of the Low Wharfs. No capacity of any kind. Cannot draw,
cannot set, was never assessed, has no entry in the Long Book.** Mother of
under-reckoner Merrow Quen, which is how she is ever in a room with the
House at all.

She does by hand what the Draw made expensive: soaks salt out of cloth over
nine days, picks rot out of grain by eye, limes a floor. Her trade was the
whole of this coast before 1010 and is now the recourse of people who cannot
afford a rate.

- **What she can say that nobody else can.** She holds the pre-Draw
  arithmetic — her mother's, and her mother's mother's — and it includes the
  fact, unwelcome and unpublished, that the Whiting was a lake within family
  memory and its crust is two hundred years old rather than eternal. She is
  also the only person in the book who describes the trade from outside it:
  *"Before the House, salt was weather. Now it's owed."*
- **Her function in both plots.** In ch 12 she gives Yannu the reason to
  believe the Whiting has a bottom. In ch 35, washing the dead of
  Sarrow-under-Wall by hand because no drawer will go near returned ground,
  she says the sentence that becomes the Break Into Three: *"It doesn't wash
  out of skin. It goes into you and stops. That's the only place it ever
  stops."*
- **Wound/Lie, briefly:** she watched her trade become a poverty and was
  told it was progress; her lie is *the ones who can do it are not better,
  they are only luckier*, which is a comfort and is not quite true, and Yannu
  is the person who complicates it for her.
- **Speech:** hours and buckets. Proverbs — the only character in the book
  who uses them.

---

## FURTHER CHARACTERS

### Halim Nesuir — 31, the betrothed

Both plots ruin and release him. Dovra's son, competent, mild, and kind in a
way that is worse than cruelty would be. He knows Sahra does not want him
and has known for eight years. He inherits four hundred tenants and a
composition he did not ask for and cannot release.

- **Ghost.** He was twelve in Ferrey when his father hanged himself, and he
  found him, and has been reasonable ever since.
- **Lie.** *If I am good enough about it, nobody will be hurt.*
- **Want.** For everyone to be all right. He wants nothing for himself in the
  whole book, which is his flaw and not his virtue.
- **Need.** To want one thing out loud.
- **Beat:** ch 17 is his scene. He would release her and cannot; the estate
  is his mother's while she lives and the forward pledge stands whoever holds
  Nesuir. He offers her the only thing in his gift — never to touch her — and
  then has to reach the alienation clause in front of her and take back the
  half he did not own, because issue outside the merger voids the composition
  for cause and the line is pledged past his mother to the House. He gives her
  the arithmetic and refuses to draw the conclusion from it, which is the most
  and the least he can do. It is meant, all of it, and it is the worst thing
  anyone says to her in the book. In ch 45, discharged, he gives her the
  tally-ring to break herself and says the first selfish sentence of his
  life, which is that he is glad and he is sorry and both are for himself.
- **Speech:** apologises mid-clause.

### Yeshin Ottun — 14, the dependent with a face

Sahra's cousin. Manifested at eleven (a spoiled apple gone clean in her
hand). Named in the composition's schedule as *the drawing line of Ottun*,
to be assessed at sixteen. If the composition holds, she is assessed against
a clean line. If it voids, she is assessed against a live entry of 2,140
carries and set to the pump: twenty years' bonded drawing in the Amrith
cistern works, which founders drawers by thirty.

She is not a symbol. She is fourteen, bored, competitive about her capacity,
proud of being useful, and entirely unaware of what her name is doing in a
schedule. In ch 21 she asks Sahra what a composition is and Sahra lies to
her. In ch 45 she is assessed against a clean line and complains about the
queue.

### Merrow Quen — 26, under-reckoner

Sefa's son; the House's man on the survey; audits the pair in ch 20, pulls
Yannu's warrants in ch 26, and is one of the two witnesses at the Wallow in
ch 44 who make the working creditable. Divided the whole way: he owes the
House his place and his mother her arithmetic, and he chooses badly twice
before he chooses well.

### Weyl Ammar — 29, hired setter to the Sarrow

The fen's setter, chronically late, chronically overworked, four spans a
year. He is what Yannu would be if Yannu took every job offered, and he is
in the book so the reader can see the ordinary version of the price before
the extraordinary one.
